title: Blending in a section, and the early unified trumpet section
summary: Blending means staying under the lead; only the earliest trumpet section tried to be one man.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Oh. Good. When you're talking about blending in, is it a matter also of tone? Is it a matter of intending your tone to blend?
Yeah. It's a matter of staying under the lead, and blending in with the lead, and blending in with the second.
Yeah. Not overshadowing where you're not supposed to.

Yeah. And then, so really when you talk about the phraseology of the section, according to number, if it was one of those pretty things, "Blues No More", or whatever. I can't remember right now. Or "The Saddest Tale", maybe. Some of those pretty things. Then Artie established the phraseology. He established the style --

-- that was coming out of the trumpet section. And you heard him, so he established the sound as well, so you got the color of the number, came out of Artie, really, didn't it. But on all numbers other than those, the phrasing, the attack, and the beat of the thing, had to come out of you.
Well, yeah. Well, I would be playing --
And that's the only time -- I will say this -- when I was there -- that's the only time that that was noticed. And you had two other guys would cooperate and do that.
The whole time I was in the band.
So in the trumpet sections that you played in in that band --
-- only that first, earliest section that you played with, that's the only section where they tried to play like one man.
Tried to be a completely unified section.
Well, Cootie, that's partly because everybody was in love with the band. Involved with the band.
Inside themselves, everybody knew what it should be. What it should sound like and should be. Right?
And there wasn't really rivalry there.
